scenes.heading: Polymers and plastics
scenes.sub: Why can some plastics be recycled but not others?
scenes.say: Drink bottles, phone cases, pipes and food wrap are all polymers. So why can some plastics be melted and recycled, while others can't?

scenes.heading: Monomers and polymers
points: Monomer: a small molecule that can join up
Polymer: thousands of monomers in a chain
Like a long chain of paperclips
scenes.say: A monomer is a small molecule that can join to many others. A polymer is a very long chain of thousands of monomers, like a chain of paperclips. Some polymers are natural, like starch and wool. Others are synthetic, like polyethene, often made from crude oil.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Party-goers let go of one drink to join a conga line
scenes.science: One bond of each C=C breaks to link monomers
scenes.breaks: People can let go and leave, but the new C–C bonds are strong covalent bonds that don't easily come apart.
scenes.say: Addition polymerisation is like a conga line. Each monomer, like ethene, has a carbon-carbon double bond. One bond breaks, like letting go of a drink with one hand, and grabs the next monomer. Nothing is lost: every atom ends up in the polymer.

scenes.heading: Making polyethene
scenes.say: Here's ethene making polyethene. The part in brackets is the repeating unit, and n is a huge number, often thousands. Notice the polymer has only single bonds. Naming is easy: poly, plus the monomer name. Ethene gives poly ethene.

scenes.heading: Find the monomer
scenes.question: A polymer has the repeating unit –(CH₂–CHCl)–. Name the monomer.
lines: Put the double bond back: CH₂=CHCl
Ethene with one H swapped for Cl
scenes.say: To find the monomer, put the double bond back between the two carbons. That gives C H two double bond C H C L: ethene with one hydrogen swapped for chlorine. It's chloroethene, and the polymer is P V C.
scenes.caption: To find the monomer, put the double bond back between the two carbons. That gives CH₂=CHCl: ethene with one hydrogen swapped for chlorine. It's chloroethene, and the polymer is PVC.

scenes.heading: Heating plastics
scenes.say: Thermoplastics are like chocolate. Their chains are held only by weak forces, so heat makes them melt, and they can be recycled. Thermosets are like a baked cake. Cross-links lock the chains, so they don't melt, they char.

scenes.heading: Plastic waste
points: Resin code helps sort for recycling
scenes.say: Most plastics aren't biodegradable, so they can last for hundreds of years. They break into tiny microplastics that spread through water and food chains. Reducing and reusing helps, and the resin code on plastics helps sort them for recycling.

Quick recap. Polymers are long chains of monomers. In addition polymerisation, the double bond opens and nothing is lost. Thermoplastics melt and can be recycled; thermosets have cross-links and char. Now try the practice questions!
